docs.title: What is a Variable?
docs.text:
A variable is a named container that stores a value in memory. In Python, variables are created the moment you assign a value to them — no explicit declaration needed.

message = "Hello, Python!"
age = 25
pi = 3.14159
is_active = True

docs.title: Variable Naming Rules
docs.text:
• Must start with a letter (a-z, A-Z) or underscore _
  • Remaining characters can be letters, digits (0-9), or underscores
  • Case-sensitive (name and Name are different)
  • Cannot use Python reserved keywords
# Valid
name = "Alice"
user_name = "Bob"
_user_id = 42
camelCase = "OK"      # not conventional in Python

# Invalid
# 1st_name = "X"     # starts with digit
# my-var = 1          # contains hyphen
# class = "math"      # reserved keyword

docs.title: Naming Conventions (PEP 8)
docs.text: Style Convention Example Variables snake_case first_name, total_count Constants UPPER_SNAKE MAX_SIZE, PI Private Leading underscore _internal Dunder Double underscores __init__

docs.title: Dynamic Typing
docs.text:
Python is dynamically typed — a variable can hold any type, and its type can change at runtime.

x = 10        # x is int
x = "hello"   # now x is str
x = [1, 2, 3] # now x is list

Use type() to check the type:

print(type(42))        # <class 'int'>
print(type("hello"))   # <class 'str'>
print(type(3.14))      # <class 'float'>

docs.title: 1. int — Integer
docs.text:
Whole numbers, positive or negative, with unlimited precision.

a = 42
b = -100
c = 0
d = 1_000_000      # underscores for readability (Python 3.6+)
e = 0x1A           # hexadecimal (26 in decimal)
f = 0b1010         # binary (10 in decimal)

print(a + b)       # -58
print(10 // 3)     # 3 (floor division)
print(10 % 3)      # 1 (modulo)
print(2 ** 10)     # 1024 (exponentiation)

docs.title: 2. float — Floating-Point Number
docs.text:
Numbers with decimal points, represented as 64-bit double-precision IEEE 754 values.

x = 3.14
y = -0.001
z = 1.0
w = 1.5e10         # scientific notation: 1.5 × 10^10 = 15000000000.0
inf = float('inf')
nan = float('nan')

print(0.1 + 0.2)                   # 0.30000000000000004 (floating-point precision!)
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 1))         # 0.3
print(isinstance(3.0, float))      # True

docs.title: 3. str — String
docs.text:
Immutable sequence of Unicode characters, enclosed in single quotes, double quotes, triple single quotes, or triple double quotes.

s1 = 'single quotes'
s2 = "double quotes"
s3 = '''triple
quotes for
multi-line'''
s4 = """also multi-line"""

# String operations
first = "Hello"
last = "World"
print(first + " " + last)        # "Hello World" (concatenation)
print("Na" * 3)                  # "NaNaNa" (repetition)

# Indexing and slicing
text = "Python"
print(text[0])      # 'P'
print(text[-1])     # 'n'
print(text[1:4])    # 'yth'  (start:stop, stop exclusive)
print(text[:3])     # 'Pyt'
print(text[::-1])   # 'nohtyP' (reverse)

# String methods
msg = "  hello, WORLD!  "
print(msg.strip())             # "hello, WORLD!"
print(msg.lower())             # "  hello, world!  "
print(msg.upper())             # "  HELLO, WORLD!  "
print(msg.replace("WORLD", "Python"))  # "  hello, Python!  "
print(msg.split(","))          # ['  hello', ' WORLD!  ']
print(", ".join(["a", "b", "c"]))  # "a, b, c"
print("hello" in msg)          # True
print(msg.startswith("  he"))  # True

# f-strings (Python 3.6+)
name = "Alice"
age = 30
print(f"{name} is {age} years old")  # "Alice is 30 years old"
print(f"{age:04d}")                  # "0030" (zero-padded)
print(f"{3.14159:.2f}")             # "3.14"

# Escape sequences
print("tab\there")
print("new\nline")
print("backslash: \\")
print('it\'s okay')

docs.title: 4. bool — Boolean
docs.text:
Represents True or False. Internally, True is 1 and False is 0.

is_sunny = True
is_raining = False

print(is_sunny and is_raining)   # False
print(is_sunny or is_raining)    # True
print(not is_sunny)              # False

# Truthy / Falsy values
print(bool(1))         # True
print(bool(0))         # False
print(bool("hello"))   # True
print(bool(""))        # False
print(bool([]))        # False
print(bool(None))      # False

docs.title: 5. NoneType — None
docs.text:
Represents the absence of a value. Only one possible value: None.

result = None
print(result)          # None
print(result is None)  # True

# Common use: placeholder or function return with no value
def find_user(id):
    return None if id <= 0 else {"id": id, "name": "Alice"}

docs.title: Type Conversion
docs.text:
Explicitly convert between types using built-in functions:

# int conversions
print(int(3.14))        # 3 (truncates decimal)
print(int("42"))        # 42
print(int(True))        # 1

# float conversions
print(float(3))         # 3.0
print(float("3.14"))    # 3.14

# str conversions
print(str(42))          # "42"
print(str(3.14))        # "3.14"
print(str(True))        # "True"

# bool conversions
print(bool(1))          # True
print(bool(0))          # False
print(bool(""))         # False
print(bool("text"))     # True

# Dangerous conversion
# int("hello")          # ValueError!

docs.title: Mutable vs Immutable
docs.text:
Type Mutable? Notes int No Every operation creates a new object float No str No Any "modification" returns a new string bool No None No list Yes dict Yes set Yes 
# Immutable — original stays unchanged
s = "hello"
s.upper()
print(s)               # "hello" (unchanged)
s = s.upper()          # reassign to capture the new string
print(s)               # "HELLO"

# id() shows object identity
x = 10
print(id(x))           # some memory address
x = x + 1
print(id(x))           # different address (new object)

docs.title: The del Statement
docs.text:
Remove a variable reference:

x = 42
print(x)    # 42
del x
# print(x)  # NameError: name 'x' is not defined

docs.title: Multiple Assignment
docs.text:
Python supports assigning to multiple variables in one line:

# Same value
a = b = c = 0

# Different values
x, y, z = 1, 2, 3

# Swapping (no temporary variable needed!)
a, b = 10, 20
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)            # 20 10

docs.title: is vs ==
docs.text:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a

print(a == b)    # True — same value
print(a is b)    # False — different objects in memory
print(a is c)    # True — same object

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
x = 10
y = 3
print(x / y)
print(x // y)
print(x % y)
print(x ** y)

What is the output?

Solution 
3.3333333333333335
3
1
1000
OperatorNameReturnsExampleResult /Divisionfloat10 / 33.333... //Floor divisionint10 // 33 %Moduloint10 % 31 **Exponentiationint/float10 ** 31000

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
What is the type of result after each line executes?

result = 42 // 5          # ?
result = 42 / 5           # ?
result = "42" + str(5)    # ?
result = bool(0)          # ?
result = None             # ?
Solution - `42 // 5` → `int` (8) - `42 / 5` → `float` (8.4) - `"42" + str(5)` → `str` ("425") - `bool(0)` → `bool` (False) - `None` → `NoneType`

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
name = "Python"
print(name[0] + name[-1])
print(name[1:4])
print(name[::-1])

What is the output?

Solution 
Pn
yth
nohtyP
- `name[0]` is `'P'`, `name[-1]` is `'n'`. - `name[1:4]` slices from index 1 up to (but not including) index 4 → `'yth'`. - `[::-1]` reverses the string.

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
a, b = 5, 10
a, b = b, a + b
print(a, b)

What is printed?

Solution 
10 15
Right-hand side is evaluated first: `(10, 5 + 10)` → `(10, 15)`, then unpacked into `a` and `b`.

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Identify the errors in the following code:

1st_number = 10
my-name = "Alice"
class = "Math"
print(MY-NAME)
Solution - `1st_number` — variable name starts with a digit. - `my-name` — hyphen is not allowed in identifiers. - `class` — reserved keyword. - `print(MY-NAME)` — variable was defined as `my-name` (which is already invalid), and `MY-NAME` is not defined.

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
text = "Data Science"
print(text.upper())
print(text.replace("Science", "Analytics"))
print(text.find("Sci"))
print("data" in text)

What is the output?

Solution 
DATA SCIENCE
Data Analytics
5
False
- `.upper()` returns a new uppercase string (original unchanged). - `.replace()` returns a new string with the substring replaced. - `.find("Sci")` returns the starting index of `"Sci"` (index 5). - `"data" in text` is `False` because strings are case-sensitive.

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
x = True
y = False
print(x and y)
print(x or y)
print(not x)
print(x + y)
print(x * 10)

What is the output?

Solution 
False
True
False
1
10
Booleans are subclasses of `int` (`True` = 1, `False` = 0), so arithmetic operations work on them.

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
What is the value of z at the end?

x = 3.14159
y = int(x)
z = float(y)
Solution 
3.0
`int(3.14159)` truncates the decimal → `3`. `float(3)` → `3.0`.

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
print(type(10))
print(type(10.0))
print(type(10 // 3))
print(type(10 / 3))
print(type("10"))

Write down the output of each print.

Solution 
<class 'int'>
<class 'float'>
<class 'int'>
<class 'float'>
<class 'str'>
- `10` is an integer literal. - `10.0` is a float literal. - `10 // 3` is integer division → `int`. - `10 / 3` always returns `float`. - `"10"` is a string literal.

docs.title: Question 10 (Challenge)
docs.text:
a = 256
b = 256
print(a is b)    # True or False?

x = 257
y = 257
print(x is y)    # True or False?

print(a == b)    # True or False?
print(x == y)    # True or False?
Solution 
True
False
True
True
Python caches small integers in the range [-5, 256] for performance. `a is b` is `True` because both point to the same cached object. `x is y` is `False` because 257 is outside the cache, so two separate objects are created. `==` compares value, so both are `True`. **Moral**: Always use `==` for value comparison; use `is` only for `None` checks.

docs.title: Collection Types Comparison
docs.text:
Feature list tuple set dict Syntax [1, 2, 3] (1, 2, 3) {1, 2, 3} {"a": 1} Ordered Yes Yes No Yes (3.7+) Mutable Yes No Yes Yes Indexed Yes Yes No By key Duplicates Allowed Allowed Not allowed Unique keys Use case Ordered sequence Fixed collection Unique items, set ops Key-value mapping 
# list — ordered, mutable, indexed
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits.append("date")
print(fruits[0])          # "apple"

# tuple — ordered, immutable, indexed
coords = (10.5, 20.3)
# coords[0] = 5.0        # TypeError!
print(coords[1])          # 20.3

# set — unordered, mutable, no duplicates
unique = {1, 2, 2, 3}
print(unique)             # {1, 2, 3}
print(1 in unique)        # True

# dict — key-value mapping, mutable
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}
person["age"] = 31
print(person.keys())      # dict_keys(['name', 'age'])

docs.title: 1 - Comparison Operators
docs.text: Operator Description Example == Equal to 5 == 5 -> True != Not equal to 5 != 3 -> True > Greater than 7 > 4 -> True < Less than 2 < 9 -> True >= Greater than or equal to 6 >= 6 -> True <= Less than or equal to 3 <= 8 -> True is True if both variables reference the same object a = [1]; b = a; a is b -> True is not True if variables reference different objects a = [1]; b = [1]; a is not b -> True in True if a value exists in a sequence 'a' in "apple" -> True not in True if a value does not exist in a sequence 'z' not in "apple" -> True

docs.title: Equal To ==
docs.text:
• 10 == 10 -> True
  • 'cat' == 'cat' -> True
  • [1, 2] == [1, 2] -> True

docs.title: Not Equal To !=
docs.text:
• 10 != 5 -> True
  • 'apple' != 'orange' -> True
  • 3 != 3 -> False

docs.title: Greater Than >
docs.text:
• 9 > 4 -> True
  • 2 > 7 -> False
  • 100 > 99 -> True

docs.title: Less Than <
docs.text:
• 1 < 8 -> True
  • 5 < 5 -> False
  • -3 < 0 -> True

docs.title: Greater Than or Equal To >=
docs.text:
• 8 >= 8 -> True
  • 9 >= 3 -> True
  • 2 >= 10 -> False

docs.title: Less Than or Equal To <=
docs.text:
• 4 <= 4 -> True
  • 1 <= 9 -> True
  • 12 <= 7 -> False

docs.title: Is (Same Object) is
docs.text:
• a = [1, 2]; b = a; a is b -> True
  • x = 256; y = 256; x is y -> True (often)
  • m = [1]; n = [1]; m is n -> False

docs.title: Is Not (Different Object) is not
docs.text:
• a = [1]; b = [1]; a is not b -> True
  • x = None; x is not None -> False
  • p = 'hi'; q = p; p is not q -> False

docs.title: In (Membership) in
docs.text:
• 'a' in 'banana' -> True
  • 3 in [1, 2, 3, 4] -> True
  • 'key' in {'key': 1, 'value': 2} -> True

docs.title: Not In (Membership) not in
docs.text:
• 'z' not in 'banana' -> True
  • 5 not in [1, 2, 3] -> True
  • 'id' not in {'name': 'Ava'} -> True

docs.title: 1) Compare strings safely (case-insensitive)
docs.text:
• 'Admin'.casefold() == 'ADMIN'.casefold() -> True
  • 'Straße'.casefold() == 'STRASSE'.casefold() -> True

docs.title: 2) Compare floats with tolerance (not strict ==)
docs.text:
• 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 -> False
  • import math; math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) -> True

docs.title: 3) Use tuple/list lexicographic comparisons
docs.text:
• (1, 9) < (2, 0) -> True
  • [1, 'a'] < [1, 'b'] -> True

docs.title: 4) Set comparisons use subset/superset meaning
docs.text:
• {1, 2} < {1, 2, 3} -> True (proper subset)
  • {1, 2} <= {1, 2} -> True (subset or equal)

docs.title: 5) Know == vs is in real code
docs.text:
• a = [1, 2]; b = [1, 2]; a == b -> True
  • a = [1, 2]; b = [1, 2]; a is b -> False
  • x = None; x is None -> True (preferred style for None checks)

docs.title: 6) Membership with dictionaries checks keys
docs.text:
• 'name' in {'name': 'Ava', 'age': 20} -> True
  • 'Ava' in {'name': 'Ava', 'age': 20} -> False

docs.title: 2 - Chained Comparisons
docs.text: Chained comparisons let you combine multiple comparisons in a single expression. For example, x < y < z means x < y and y < z, but y is evaluated only once. Python evaluates chained comparisons from left to right and stops as soon as one part is False.

docs.title: Chained Comparison Examples
docs.text:
• 1 < 5 < 10 -> True
  • score = 85; 0 <= score <= 100 -> True
  • a, b, c = 2, 5, 3; a < b > c -> True
age = 25
is_valid_age = 18 <= age < 65
print(is_valid_age)

Output:

True

docs.title: 3 - Conditional Statements
docs.text: Conditional statements let your program make decisions. Use if to check a condition, elif for additional conditions, and else for a fallback case. Python uses indentation to define each block, so spacing is required and meaningful.

docs.title: 1) Basic if
docs.text:
temperature = 34

if temperature > 30:
    print("It is a hot day")

Output:

It is a hot day

docs.title: 2) if + else
docs.text:
number = 7

if number % 2 == 0:
    print("Even")
else:
    print("Odd")

Output:

Odd

docs.title: 3) if + elif + else
docs.text:
marks = 82

if marks >= 90:
    print("Grade A")
elif marks >= 75:
    print("Grade B")
else:
    print("Grade C")

Output:

Grade B

docs.title: 4) Multiple conditions with and
docs.text:
age = 20
has_id = True

if age >= 18 and has_id:
    print("Entry allowed")
else:
    print("Entry denied")

Output:

Entry allowed

docs.title: 4 - Loops
docs.text: Loops let you run a block of code multiple times without writing the same lines again. In Python, the two main loop types are for (iterate over items) and while (repeat while a condition is True). You can also control loops using break (stop early) and continue (skip current iteration).

docs.title: The range() Function
docs.text:
range() is used to generate a sequence of numbers, mostly inside for loops. The stop value is not included in the result.

  • range(stop) -> starts from 0 and goes up to stop - 1
  • range(start, stop) -> starts from start and goes up to stop - 1
  • range(start, stop, step) -> moves by step each time (step can be negative)
print(list(range(5)))
print(list(range(2, 6)))
print(list(range(10, 2, -2)))

Output:

[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
[2, 3, 4, 5]
[10, 8, 6, 4]

docs.title: 1) for loop with a list
docs.text:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]

for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

Output:

apple
banana
mango

docs.title: 2) for loop with range()
docs.text:
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)

Output:

1
2
3
4
5

docs.title: 1) for loop to sum even numbers
docs.text:
numbers = [12, 7, 5, 10, 8]
total = 0

for n in numbers:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        total += n

print("Sum of even numbers:", total)

Output:

Sum of even numbers: 30

docs.title: 2) while loop for factorial
docs.text:
n = 5
factorial = 1

while n > 1:
    factorial *= n
    n -= 1

print("Factorial:", factorial)

Output:

Factorial: 120

docs.title: 1) for + else to check prime number
docs.text:
n = 29

for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
    if n % i == 0:
        print(n, "is not prime")
        break
else:
    print(n, "is prime")

Output:

29 is prime

docs.title: 2) while + else for retry logic
docs.text:
attempt = 1
max_attempts = 3
pin = "2580"
entered_pin = ["1111", "9999", "2580"]

while attempt <= max_attempts:
    current = entered_pin[attempt - 1]
    if current == pin:
        print("Access granted on attempt", attempt)
        break
    print("Wrong PIN on attempt", attempt)
    attempt += 1
else:
    print("Card blocked")

Output:

Wrong PIN on attempt 1
Wrong PIN on attempt 2
Access granted on attempt 3

docs.title: 3) Nested for loops for matrix transpose
docs.text:
matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
transpose = []

for col in range(len(matrix[0])):
    new_row = []
    for row in range(len(matrix)):
        new_row.append(matrix[row][col])
    transpose.append(new_row)

print(transpose)

Output:

[[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]

docs.title: 4) while loop
docs.text:
count = 1

while count <= 3:
    print("Count:", count)
    count += 1

Output:

Count: 1
Count: 2
Count: 3

docs.title: 5) break and continue
docs.text:
for n in range(1, 8):
    if n == 3:
        continue  # skip 3
    if n == 6:
        break  # stop loop at 6
    print(n)

Output:

1
2
4
5

docs.title: 6) for loop with enumerate()
docs.text:
enumerate() lets you loop through items and their index at the same time (start=1 begins indexing from 1).

colors = ["red", "green", "blue"]

for index, color in enumerate(colors, start=1):
    print(index, color)

Output:

1 red
2 green
3 blue

docs.title: 7) Loop through dictionary items
docs.text:
student = {"name": "Ava", "age": 20, "grade": "A"}

for key, value in student.items():
    print(key, "->", value)

Output:

name -> Ava
age -> 20
grade -> A

docs.title: 8) Nested for loops
docs.text:
for i in range(1, 4):
    for j in range(1, 4):
        print(i, "x", j, "=", i * j)

Output:

1 x 1 = 1
1 x 2 = 2
1 x 3 = 3
2 x 1 = 2
2 x 2 = 4
2 x 3 = 6
3 x 1 = 3
3 x 2 = 6
3 x 3 = 9

docs.title: 9) while True with break
docs.text:
num = 1

while True:
    print(num)
    num += 1
    if num > 5:
        break

Output:

1
2
3
4
5

docs.title: 5 - Functions in Python
docs.text: Functions are reusable blocks of code that perform a specific task. In Python, you define a function using the def keyword. Functions can take inputs (parameters), can return output using return, and help avoid repeating the same logic.

docs.title: Basic Function Syntax
docs.text:
def function_name(parameters):
    # function body
    return value  # optional

docs.title: 1) Function with no parameters and no return value
docs.text:
def greet():
    print("Hello, learner!")


greet()

Output:

Hello, learner!

docs.title: 2) Function with parameters and return value
docs.text:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b


result = add(10, 5)
print(result)

Output:

15

docs.title: 3) Function with default argument
docs.text:
def power(base, exponent=2):
    return base ** exponent


print(power(4))
print(power(4, 3))

Output:

16
64

docs.title: 4) Function called with keyword arguments
docs.text:
def introduce(name, city):
    print(name, "lives in", city)


introduce(city="Lahore", name="Ava")

Output:

Ava lives in Lahore

docs.title: 5) Function with variable positional arguments (*args)
docs.text:
def total_sum(*numbers):
    return sum(numbers)


print(total_sum(1, 2, 3))
print(total_sum(10, 20, 30, 40))

Output:

6
100

docs.title: 6) Function with variable keyword arguments (**kwargs)
docs.text:
def show_profile(**details):
    for key, value in details.items():
        print(key, "->", value)


show_profile(name="Ava", role="Engineer", experience=3)

Output:

name -> Ava
role -> Engineer
experience -> 3

docs.title: 7) Function returning multiple values
docs.text:
def min_max(values):
    return min(values), max(values)


smallest, largest = min_max([12, 4, 19, 7])
print("Min:", smallest)
print("Max:", largest)

Output:

Min: 4
Max: 19

docs.title: 8) Recursive function
docs.text:
def factorial(n):
    if n == 0 or n == 1:
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)


print(factorial(5))

Output:

120

docs.title: 6 - Lambda Function
docs.text: Lambda functions are small anonymous functions created with the lambda keyword. They can take multiple arguments, but they can contain only one expression. They are useful for short operations, especially with sorted(), map(), and filter().

docs.title: Lambda Function Syntax
docs.text: lambda arguments: expression

docs.title: 1) Add two numbers
docs.text:
add = lambda a, b: a + b
print(add(4, 6))

Output:

10

docs.title: 2) Square a number
docs.text:
square = lambda n: n * n
print(square(7))

Output:

49

docs.title: 3) Use lambda with sorted()
docs.text:
students = [("Ava", 22), ("Zain", 19), ("Mina", 21)]
by_age = sorted(students, key=lambda item: item[1])
print(by_age)

Output:

[('Zain', 19), ('Mina', 21), ('Ava', 22)]

docs.title: 4) Use lambda with map()
docs.text:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]
doubled = list(map(lambda x: x * 2, numbers))
print(doubled)

Output:

[2, 4, 6, 8]

docs.title: 5) Use lambda with filter()
docs.text:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
evens = list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, numbers))
print(evens)

Output:

[2, 4, 6]

docs.title: 6) Lambda with conditional expression
docs.text:
label = lambda n: "positive" if n > 0 else "zero" if n == 0 else "negative"
print(label(-3))
print(label(0))
print(label(8))

Output:

negative
zero
positive

docs.title: When Not to Use Lambda
docs.text:
Use a normal def function instead of lambda when:

  • The logic needs multiple statements (loops, try/except, multiple return points).
  • The expression becomes too long and hurts readability.
  • You want a clear function name for debugging, stack traces, or reuse.
  • You want to add a docstring or type hints for better documentation.
# Less readable with lambda
result = list(map(lambda n: n * 2 if n % 2 == 0 else n * 3, [1, 2, 3, 4]))


# Clearer with def
def transform(n):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n * 2
    return n * 3


result = list(map(transform, [1, 2, 3, 4]))
print(result)

Output:

[3, 4, 9, 8]

docs.title: What Is a Python Package?
docs.text:
A Python package is a way to organize related Python code in folders. It usually contains one or more Python modules (.py files) and often an __init__.py file.

  • Module: a single Python file (for example, math_utils.py)
  • Package: a folder that groups related modules (for example, my_project/utils/)

Packages help you:

  • keep code organized,
  • reuse code across projects,
  • and share code with others.

docs.title: 1) Standard Library Packages (built into Python)
docs.text:
Examples: math, os, json, datetime

import math

print(math.sqrt(25))

docs.title: 2) Third-Party Packages (installed from PyPI)
docs.text:
Examples: numpy, pandas, requests, matplotlib

Install them with pip:

python -m pip install numpy pandas requests

docs.title: 1) NumPy
docs.text:
NumPy is used for fast numerical computing and arrays.

import numpy as np

arr = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(arr.mean())
print(arr.sum())

Output:

25.0
100

docs.title: 2) Pandas
docs.text:
Pandas is used for data analysis with tables (DataFrame).

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "name": ["Ava", "Zain", "Mina"],
        "score": [85, 92, 78],
    }
)

print(df)
print(df["score"].mean())

Output:

   name  score
0   Ava     85
1  Zain     92
2  Mina     78
85.0

docs.title: 3) Requests
docs.text:
requests is used to send HTTP requests to APIs and websites.

import requests

response = requests.get("https://api.github.com")
print(response.status_code)

Possible output:

200

docs.title: How to Install These Packages
docs.text:
You can install numpy, pandas, and requests using either command:

python -m pip install numpy pandas requests
pip install numpy pandas requests

Both commands are valid. Use python -m pip when you want to be sure packages are installed in the same Python interpreter you are running. Use pip as a shorter command when your environment is already set correctly.

docs.title: Command Breakdown
docs.text:
For these commands:

python -m pip install numpy pandas requests
pip install numpy pandas requests
  • python: runs the Python interpreter.
  • -m: tells Python to run a module as a script.
  • pip: the module being run (pip package manager).
  • install: the pip action to install packages.
  • numpy pandas requests: package names to install.

In pip install ..., pip directly runs the pip executable from your current environment.

Why use python -m pip instead of just pip?

  • It ensures pip runs with the same Python interpreter/environment you selected.
  • This helps avoid installing packages into the wrong Python version.

You can also install them one by one:

python -m pip install numpy
python -m pip install pandas
python -m pip install requests

To check if installation worked:

python -m pip show numpy pandas requests

docs.title: 1) List installed packages
docs.text: python -m pip list

docs.title: 2) Check pip version
docs.text: python -m pip --version

docs.title: 3) Upgrade a package
docs.text: python -m pip install --upgrade numpy

docs.title: 4) Uninstall a package
docs.text: python -m pip uninstall requests

docs.title: 5) Save current environment packages
docs.text: python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt

docs.title: 6) Install from a requirements.txt file
docs.text: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: 7) Check dependency issues
docs.text: python -m pip check

docs.title: Quick Summary
docs.text:
• A package is a collection of related modules.
  • Use built-in packages for common tasks.
  • Install third-party packages with pip.
  • Common beginner-friendly packages: numpy, pandas, and requests.

docs.title: Introduction to Agentic AI and Data Roles
What is Agentic AI?
docs.text: Agentic AI is an AI system that can do more than give a single reply. It can take your prompt as a goal, plan steps, use tools, perform actions, check results, and keep going step by step until the job is completed.

docs.title: One-line definition
docs.text: Agentic AI is goal-driven AI that uses prompts, planning, tools, memory, and feedback loops to take multi-step actions and complete tasks with minimal human guidance.

docs.title: 1) Prompt
docs.text:
A prompt is your instruction to the AI.

Example prompt:

"Find 3 beginner courses on AI and make a 6-month study plan."

docs.title: 2) Goal and constraints
docs.text:
From your prompt, the AI identifies:

  • The main goal (what to achieve)
  • The limits (time, budget, format, and rules)

docs.title: 3) Planning
docs.text:
Instead of answering immediately, it creates a small plan.

Example:

  1. Search courses
  2. Compare courses
  3. Build a schedule
  4. Present the final plan

docs.title: 4) Tools
docs.text:
Tools are extra abilities the AI can use outside normal text generation.

Examples of tools:

  • Web search
  • Calculator
  • Code execution
  • File reading and writing
  • Calling APIs
  • Database lookup

Without tools, AI can mostly "talk." With tools, AI can also "do."

docs.title: 5) Actions
docs.text: The AI runs those tools to collect real information or perform real tasks.

docs.title: 6) Observation and feedback
docs.text:
After each action, it reads the result and checks:

  • Did it work?
  • Is anything missing?
  • Did an error happen?

Then it adjusts the next step.

docs.title: 7) Memory
docs.text:
The AI keeps useful context while working.

  • Short-term memory: what happened during this task
  • Long-term memory (if enabled): user preferences and past decisions

docs.title: 8) Decision loop
docs.text:
It repeats this cycle:

Plan → Act → Check → Improve

This loop continues until the goal is reached or the process is stopped.

docs.title: 9) Guardrails and human control
docs.text:
Good agentic systems include safety controls, such as:

  • Permission checks
  • Blocked actions for risky operations
  • Human approval for sensitive steps

docs.title: Quick difference
docs.text: A normal chatbot mostly gives one response. Agentic AI can run a workflow from start to finish.

docs.title: Data Analyst vs Data Engineer vs Data Scientist
docs.text: This image compares three common careers in the data world. They all work with data, but each role solves a different part of the problem.

docs.title: Data Analyst
docs.text:
Main focus: understanding what already happened.

  • Helps teams make decisions using reports and dashboards
  • Finds trends and patterns in historical data
  • Common skills: SQL, Excel, Power BI or Tableau, and basic statistics

Simple question they answer: "What is happening in the business right now?"

docs.title: Data Engineer
docs.text:
Main focus: building the data foundation.

  • Creates and maintains data pipelines (automatic data movement systems)
  • Cleans and transforms raw data so others can use it safely
  • Sets up storage systems like data warehouses and data lakes
  • Common skills: Python, ETL tools, big data systems, and cloud platforms

Simple question they answer: "How do we make data reliable and ready to use?"

docs.title: Data Scientist
docs.text:
Main focus: predicting what is likely to happen next.

  • Builds machine learning models
  • Uses statistics and experiments to test ideas
  • Creates predictive systems (for example: demand forecast, churn prediction)
  • Common skills: Python or R, machine learning, statistics, and visualization

Simple question they answer: "What will probably happen next, and why?"

docs.title: How these roles connect
docs.text:
In most teams, the flow looks like this:

Raw Data → Data Engineer prepares it → Data Analyst explains it → Data Scientist predicts with it

In small companies, one person may do parts of all three roles. In larger companies, these are usually separate jobs.
